summary:
An intelligent monitoring system
We leverage assets already available to NASA: sensors, cameras, logs, microphones, and specialized hardware.
We have developed AI models that monitor astronauts in real time. The system establishes a baseline for each astronaut, detects anomalous patterns and symptoms, and generates predictions. Relevant information is relayed as alerts and recommendations to the Crew Medical Officer and medical specialists on Earth.
How do we address this challenge?
The challenge explicitly notes that during long-duration missions, astronauts are exposed to hostile conditions that can severely compromise their health—yet the astronauts themselves remain directly responsible for their own medical check-ups.
Our system collects, analyzes, and predicts health data, displaying it in real time to both the astronauts and medical specialists.
Why it matters:
During the Crew-11 mission in January 2026, astronaut Michael Ficke lost the ability to speak for 20 minutes. This forced a complete overhaul of station operations, led to the cancellation of a scheduled extravehicular activity (EVA), and resulted in the crew of four returning to Earth a month early.
Incidents like these continue to recur:
During the Crew-8 mission (2024), an astronaut required hospitalization. Recurrent medical issues—such as venous thrombosis and severe SANS (Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome)—all point to a clear problem:
There is no intelligent monitoring system in place.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Healt Monitoring is a health monitoring system for astronauts with three parts. The first is AZRIEL, a wearable prototype worn on the forearm and built as two stacked boards inside a case. It measures heart rate and blood oxygen (SpO2) with a MAX30102, body temperature with a MAX30205, and movement and activity with an MPU6050 accelerometer and gyroscope. An ESP32-WROOM-32 reads the sensors, and a 0.96" OLED screen (SSD1306) shows the readings on the device itself.

The second part is the ground viewer, a dashboard for the doctor on Earth, connected to a Supabase database. The doctor can browse astronauts, missions, crews, devices and historical events. They can follow telemetry over time, including heart rate, SpO2, temperature, respiration, blood pressure, motion and signal quality, and review alerts by severity together with their telemetry evidence and the interventions taken. They can also run mission simulations in the browser. These use a reproducible seed and generate physiologically plausible, correlated signals. A Hardware tab shows AZRIEL in an interactive 3D model, from the closed case down to each component, along with photos of the real build.

The third part is the space viewer, for the doctor on board. Using only a regular camera, it tracks up to two people at once and shows their indicators next to the image. It also estimates body mass and displays a 3D muscle twin that follows the person's posture. When a value becomes critical, the platform warns the crew with sirens and a spoken message. Every value is labeled as real (measured by a device), reconstructed (estimated to recreate a historical event) or synthetic (generated for a simulation), so a simulation is never confused with a real measurement.

What benefits does it offer?

It catches changes in vital signs early, before they become emergencies. It makes the crew more independent, which matters on long missions where communication with Earth is delayed. Both doctors see the same information, each through a view designed for their role. The camera features need no extra hardware, and AZRIEL uses low-cost, off-the-shelf parts, so it is easy to replicate.

What is the expected impact?

Healt Monitoring is a step toward safer long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars, where crews have to manage their own health. The same approach also applies on Earth: remote patient monitoring, isolated places such as Antarctic bases or rural areas, and athletes or workers in extreme conditions.

What tools, programming languages, hardware or software did we use?

Hardware: ESP32-WROOM-32, MAX30102, MAX30205, MPU6050, OLED SSD1306, perfboards, wiring and a protective case. Firmware: C++ with Arduino for the ESP32. Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS. 3D and animation: three.js, React Three Fiber, Motion and anime.js. Computer vision: Google MediaPipe Pose Landmarker, running in the browser. Data and charts: Supabase (PostgreSQL) and Recharts. Voice: text-to-speech for spoken alerts. Deployment and teamwork: Vercel and GitHub.

How is the project creative?

It brings a physical wearable, computer vision and 3D visualization together in one platform. It turns a regular camera into a measuring tool. It reflects how real missions work, with one doctor on Earth and another in space, each with their own view. Its interactive 3D model lets anyone see how the device is built, piece by piece, and its sound and voice alerts mean the crew doesn't need to be looking at a screen.

What factors did our team consider?

Safety and ethics: the system supports decisions and does not diagnose, and its alerts are not clinical decisions. Data honesty: every value is labeled with its source, and missing data is shown as missing, never replaced with zero. Privacy: camera processing happens in the browser, and the published photos have their metadata removed. Reproducibility: simulations use seeds, so they can be repeated exactly. Accessibility: the platform works in English and Spanish, and its visual and sound alerts are easy to understand. Cost and wearability: affordable parts and a compact design that can be worn on the forearm.
